title: The 28th of September
subject: One picture, every reason to celebrate
blurb: Every one of these is a real thing somebody celebrates on the 28th of September - and one of them is a birthday. They are all in the picture. Name the missing word in each.

items.spot: The steamship at the top left, with small children carrying suitcases up the gangway.
items.hint: Four letters, and a bitterly ironic one: over 100,000 children were shipped from Britain to the Commonwealth, many told they were orphans when they were not.
items.note: Marked in Canada. The migration ran from 1869 into the late 1940s.

items.spot: The rain cloud up in the sky with a bright gold edge, and someone below it grinning anyway.
items.hint: Six letters. The proverb says silver; the day upgrades it.

items.spot: The window with a service banner hanging in it, a single gold star at its centre.
items.hint: Seven letters. The gold star in the window means a child who did not come home from service.
items.note: Observed on the last Sunday in September. The banner tradition dates from the First World War.

items.spot: The desk of six screens covered in red and green candlesticks, top right.
items.hint: Four letters, short for a longer word. Trading the firm's own money rather than a client's.

items.spot: The state outline pinned to the wall, with a tiny biplane over it and a red cardinal perched on the frame.
items.hint: Two words, fourteen letters. First in flight, and there is another state directly above it.
items.note: The National Day Calendar works through the states in the order they joined the Union. The biplane is Kitty Hawk, 1903.

items.spot: The glass-fronted town hall with a magnifying glass held up to it.
items.hint: Four letters. The campaign for open government: what the public is entitled to do about what the state is up to.
items.note: Started in Sofia in 2002 by freedom-of-information campaigners, and runs alongside the UNESCO day.

items.template: International Day for Universal Access to ___
items.spot: The library desk with the big lowercase i above it, and a wall of open filing drawers.
items.hint: Eleven letters. UNESCO says you have a right to seek it, receive it and pass it on.
items.note: Proclaimed by UNESCO in 2019, though the date had been marked unofficially since 2002.

items.spot: Two people leaning over a garden fence with mugs of tea, left of the houses.
items.hint: Eight letters the American way, and the person on the other side of that fence.
items.note: Spelled the American way on the calendar; the game takes the British spelling too.

items.spot: The classroom: one hand up, and an enormous question mark on the blackboard.
items.hint: Six letters. Teachers invented the day to get children over the fear of asking one.
items.note: The usual line is that there is no such thing. The day exists because children do not believe it.

items.spot: The aquarium done up as a theatre: tiny curtains, a spotlight, and fish taking the stage.
items.hint: Nine letters, one word. Turn the lights down and let the fish perform.

items.spot: Bottom left: a vet in a white coat holding a syringe, and one very brave dog.
items.hint: A disease you catch from an animal bite. The date is the anniversary of the death of the man who made the vaccine.
items.note: 28 September is the day Louis Pasteur died. He developed the first rabies vaccine in 1885.

items.spot: Two hands passing a loaf of bread over an empty bowl, middle left.
items.hint: What an empty bowl means. The day is about food insecurity and what is being done about it.

items.spot: The open-roofed hut in the garden, palm fronds across the top, a family eating underneath.
items.hint: Six letters. A Jewish festival lasting seven days, during which meals are eaten in a temporary hut built for the purpose.
items.note: The hut is a sukkah; its roof must be loose enough to see the stars through. It falls in the autumn, and can land in late September.

items.spot: Everyone round the kitchen table with a roast in the middle, centre of the picture.
items.hint: Six letters. The point of the day is that you all sit down and eat a home-cooked meal together.
items.note: Observed on the fourth Monday in September.

items.template: Read a Child a ___ You Like Day
items.spot: The armchair with an adult and a small child sharing something with pictures in it.
items.hint: Four letters. The catch is that it has to be one of your own childhood favourites, not theirs.

items.spot: The parent and boy throwing a ball to each other on the grass.
items.hint: Four letters. There is a day for the other one in March.

items.spot: The pint glass on the pub table, bottom right of centre, with a good head on it.
items.hint: Four letters. Needs no explanation.

items.spot: The bowl of rice topped with pink cubes of raw fish, avocado and seaweed.
items.hint: Four letters, two syllables, and Hawaiian. Raw fish, rice, and a queue outside at lunchtime.
items.note: It means 'to slice' or 'cut crosswise' in Hawaiian, and it rhymes with 'okay' rather than with 'joke'.

items.spot: The pie on the windowsill, red fruit and a swirl of cream on top.
items.hint: Ten letters. The red one. Not technically a berry, which nobody cares about today.

items.spot: Bottom right: a film star with a great deal of hair and a pair of dark glasses, beside a clapperboard.
items.hint: A French actress of the fifties and sixties who walked away from it at 39 and has spent the fifty years since campaigning for animals.
items.note: Born in Paris in 1934. She made her last film in 1973 and founded her animal welfare foundation in 1986.
